rv.q: Abounding with witty entertainment and curiosity value, augmented by scene-stealing appearances from two real-life corgis, it confirms the promise shown by Marcelo Dos Santos with his comic monologue
There's something gleefully subversive about Dos Santos's script and Grandage's bouncy production, which makes it compelling.

Evans — who, like the real Billy, boasts a magnificent mane of ebony hair — then prepares us for the QM's entrance by elaborating on her legend for being a thirsty old dear. Despite her twinkly appearance, she could toss back the cocktails with what else but gay abandon.

Emily Barber memorably doubles up as a sitcom actress and a bonkers aristo. But my abiding memory is of the QM serenely holding a dildo-shaped sculpture made by a fake African prince. It’s all just froth - but there’s a dash of bitters at the end to keep this comic cocktail from cloying.

He is camp and chirpy in Evans’s bouncy performance, which relishes the sharp wit of Marcelo Dos Santos’s script. Eventually his royal mistress arrives and it is evident that Billy and HM are quite the double act.

Certainly it helps that Penelope Wilton and Luke Evans play the leads. That the always excellent Wilton makes big funny lines feel casual and intimate comes as a joy, but not a surprise. Her Queen Mother, whom we meet aged 79 at Clarence House in April 1979, is a figure of perennial wit and fitful pique (do not underboil Her Majesty’s eggs).
The shift between farce and the more nuanced drama can be jarring. Yet overall Grandage’s production executes itself as nimbly as clockwork, delivering plenty of laughs along with the live corgis.
Grandage’s production is consistently funny, and the performances entertain, but this play really doesn’t know what it’s saying.

Billy, for his part, finds a place where he can reinvent himself, from working-class youth to powerful confidant. He is first seen orchestrating a floral display with the imperious punctiliousness of an autocratic conductor and manages to combine haughty grandeur with both a twinkle and a hint of insecurity.
This is the epitome of theatre as light entertainment.

This impeccably played comedy of manners nicely balances palace gossip with broader ideas about class, power, and way that tradition can both comfort and stifle...We can’t live in the past forever, but this lively visit is a right royal romp.
This right royal romp is uproariously funny but also gives a fascinating insight to the inner workings of that famous family.
Wilton and Evans are a delightful duo, bouncing off each other effortlessly.
The performances could not be better.
'Backstairs Billy', for all its humour, feels like a smudged snapshot rather than a fully realised portrait.

cn.t: Critics find this witty royal household comedy a light, entertaining evening with sharp one-liners and live corgis, though tonal shifts can jar. The blend of laughs and underlying melancholy lingers after curtain call.
